description: Machine-readable open-decision register. A question is RESOLVED only when an existing declaration already answers it; otherwise it is recorded with the arbiter it needs, the evidence gathered, the current interpretation and what is blocked until it is decided. Every row carries owner, affected domains, current interpretation, decision required, blocking level, date and references, so a future agent can continue without the historical chat. Nothing here is a silent choice.

decisions.question: Are the `lego.*` error codes named by the backend degradation vocabulary published?
decisions.resolution: Resolved by publishing the codes, not by removing the names. `contracts/errors.contract.json` went 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0 (a MINOR change: codes were added, none removed or redefined) and now publishes 35 codes, of which 11 are in the `lego` namespace: lego.access_denied, lego.backpressure, lego.cancelled, lego.capability_unavailable, lego.deadline_exceeded, lego.dependency_disabled, lego.interaction_mismatch, lego.migration_required, lego.operation_unsupported, lego.unavailable, lego.version_incompatible. Each carries `retryable` and a `retryRationale`. The registry rule that a code's namespace must equal a domain's declared `errorNamespace` is satisfied: domain `lego-foundation` declares `errorNamespace: "lego"`. All four codes named in the original finding (lego.capability_unavailable, lego.version_incompatible, lego.dependency_disabled, lego.migration_required) are published, so the degradation actions in interaction.mjs no longer name a code a consumer cannot look up.

decisions.question: Who owns the AI vocabulary - the frontend or the AI Foundation LEGO?
decisions.resolution: The manager owns it, as of P2.10: contract `ai.foundation@1.0.0` (domain `ai-foundation`, owner `manager`, status `contract-only`) declares the taxonomy, five provider kinds, eleven `ai.*` capability contracts, the 26 agent-event types, the trace/delegation/approval/artifact/context fields and the transport ladder. decisions.question: Which permission namespace do AI capabilities use?
decisions.finding: Two namespaces exist for the same grants. The published AI operations require 22 `ai:*` names (`ai:model:invoke`, `ai:agent:invoke`, `ai:agent:delegate`, `ai:app:read`, ...), while the six frontend AI capabilities declare `inference:invoke`, `agent:run`, `agent:observe`, `agent:delegate`, `workflow:write` and `execution:escalate`. Four of the six are the same grant as a published `ai:*` name; `workflow:write` and `execution:escalate` name grants whose domains publish no permission names at all.

vocabulary.mjs -> local set `frontendCapabilityPermission`, four values mapped into `aiPermission`, two declared with reasons
decisions.frontendBehaviour: Nothing is renamed silently. The lock declares the mapping (`inference:invoke -> ai:model:invoke`, `agent:run -> ai:agent:invoke`, `agent:observe -> ai:agent:read`, `agent:delegate -> ai:agent:delegate`), each unmapped word carries the reason it exists, and the frontend refuses an undeclared permission word instead of accepting it as a synonym.

decisions.question: Which Skill operation set and contract version are canonical, now that an implementation exists?
decisions.resolution: Resolved by adopting the actual tested P2.12 shape rather than the larger proposed one. Canonical contract is ai.skill@1.0.0, owner manager, on the existing ai-foundation domain, now locked in apps/n8n-lego/src/lego/contracts/contract-lock.json. Canonical published operations are exactly four: skill.list, skill.resolve, skill.describe, skill.validate-selection. skill.register, skill.select, skill.load and skill.release were NOT published: they are internal lifecycle methods of the registry object. Publishing load would make lazy discovery a caller concern and defeat it; publishing register would let any caller mutate the vocabulary other consumers negotiate against. There is no execute operation and no ai:skill:execute permission, because execution is not a skill operation and no published name may imply that it is. The drift this row records — documents describing a Skill surface that did not match the code — is closed by locking the implemented shape so consumers have one published vocabulary.
decisions.historicalFinding: Agent 1's frontend planning documents described Skill as publicationPending under XA-11 with a broader, proposed operation surface, while the P2.12 backend implemented and tested a narrower four-operation registry. Two descriptions of the same concept existed and a consumer had no way to tell which was authoritative.

decisions.frontendConsumption: Consumer side closed in P2.12 finalize: packages/frontend-lego quotes ai.skill@1.0.0 (four operations, six states, four disclosure levels, two permission words), the publication block names the row it was verified against, and the alignment test requires exact agreement. No frontend vocabulary was invented to bridge the difference, and none is left to bridge.

rules: A resolved row cites an existing declaration; an open row names its arbiter and what is blocked.
The frontend never picks a new shared word to end an open question — it fails closed and records the question.
A finding stays in the record after it is fixed, so the reasoning survives the fix.
The record is checked by tests: the lock is compared against the backend modules when they are present (test/29), and every open row states what the frontend does meanwhile.

A vocabulary quoted from a file with no publishing contract carries a structured `publicationPending` record naming the owner, the domain and a recorded decision - a free-text note is not enough, and an invented contract row is worse.
Every row names its owner, its affected domains, its current interpretation, the decision it requires, its blocking level and its references - a row without those is incomplete.
A superseded row is kept with a pointer to what replaced it; deleting history is not allowed.

alignment.how: The lock quotes values with provenance (contract id, version, owner, file, declaration). The test reads that declaration and compares the values, and it also compares the quoted *semantics* (the degradation actions and the callable lifecycle states). It skips with a stated reason only when the backend foundation is not on this branch at all; pointing `N8N_BACKEND_LEGO_ROOT` at a fetched backend tree runs it for real, and then a missing file is a failure, never a skip. The comparison itself is exercised (a renamed, a missing and an invented term must all be reported), so a pass means the check ran.
alignment.whenItRunsFully: after the backend foundation (apps/n8n-lego/src/lego/**, Agent 2) is on this branch
